title: The English Lantern Clock
body:
Specifications: The English lantern clock is a brass, weight-driven clock of the seventeenth century, named for its lantern-like shape: four brass pillars at the corners, a domed or flat top with finials, and fretted side panels. It typically stands 30 to 40 centimetres tall and was made to sit on a wall bracket or a shelf.

Mechanism: Lantern clocks are driven by weights hanging on gut lines or ropes, and the earliest ones have no pendulum at all. They were the first widely owned domestic clocks in England, made from about 1600 onward, and they struck the hour on a bell.

Maintenance: Keep a lantern clock level, wind it by pulling the weights, and dust the brass with a soft dry cloth. Never polish engraved brass aggressively, since the engraving is shallow and easily removed.

Build and restoration: Restoration starts with photographing the movement and noting which parts are original, since many lantern clocks were later converted. Tools: screwdrivers, soft cloth, oil, tweezers, and magnification.

title: The Verge and Foliot
body:
Specifications: The earliest lantern clocks are regulated by a verge escapement with a foliot balance: a horizontal bar with adjustable weights at each end, rocking back and forth on the verge arbor. There is no pendulum, and the timekeeping is rough by modern standards, often gaining or losing a quarter hour a day.

Mechanism: The verge arbor carries two pallets that alternately engage a crown wheel, and the foliot's inertia sets the beat rate. Moving the foliot weights outward slows the beat, and moving them inward speeds it, which is how the clock is regulated.

Maintenance: Regulate a foliot clock by moving both weights equally, a little at a time, and timing the clock over a full day. Keep the crown wheel teeth and pallets clean and lightly oiled, since dirt changes the beat more than in a pendulum clock.

Build and restoration: Foliot repair means checking the verge pallets for wear and the foliot bar for straightness. Tools: tweezers, oil, magnification, timing chart, and a verge depth gauge.

title: Weight Drive and Gut Lines
body:
Specifications: Lantern clocks are driven by weights, usually lead cylinders in brass cases, hanging on gut lines or ropes wound around barrels in the movement. One weight drives the going train and one drives the strike train, and each falls as the clock runs.

Mechanism: As a weight falls it turns its barrel, and the barrel's great wheel drives the going or strike train. Gut lines were later replaced by brass chains or steel cables in many surviving clocks, but the drive principle is unchanged.

Maintenance: Wind a lantern clock by pulling the free end of each line until the weight is fully raised, and never let a weight drop to the floor. Check gut lines for fraying at least once a year, since a broken line drops the weight and can damage the case.

Build and restoration: Replacing a gut line means winding the new line evenly on the barrel and tying it with a secure knot. Tools: gut line or cable, tweezers, screwdrivers, oil, and a weight scale.

title: The Single-Hand Dial
body:
Specifications: Early lantern clocks have a single hand, the hour hand, because their timekeeping was too rough for minutes to mean anything. The dial is a brass chapter ring with Roman numerals and a quarter-hour division, and the hand points to the hour and the nearest quarter.

Mechanism: The hour hand is fixed to the hour wheel arbor and turns once every twelve hours, driven from the going train through the motion work. Later lantern clocks added a minute hand when pendulum conversions improved their accuracy.

Maintenance: Read a single-hand dial by the hour numeral and the quarter marks, and set it by moving the hand to the correct hour. Do not force the hand backwards against the strike release.

Build and restoration: Single-hand dials are cleaned with a soft dry brush only. Tools: soft brush, screwdrivers, oil, and a dial template.

title: The Chapter Ring and Engraved Dial
body:
Specifications: The lantern clock dial is a brass chapter ring, engraved with Roman numerals, half-hour and quarter-hour marks, and often a maker's name and a town in the centre. The centre may be engraved with a rose, a tulip, or a coat of arms.

Mechanism: The chapter ring is screwed to the movement's front plate, and the hand turns over it from the hour wheel arbor. Engraving was done by hand, so the lettering varies from clock to clock and is a useful clue to the maker.

Maintenance: Clean an engraved dial with a soft dry brush, never with polish or water, since both remove the dark wax in the engraving that makes the letters readable. Tarnish that will not brush away is best left alone.

Build and restoration: Re-waxing engraving is done with black wax rubbed into the lines and wiped from the surface. Tools: soft brush, black wax, cloth, and magnification.

title: Countwheel Striking
body:
Specifications: Lantern clocks strike the hour using a countwheel: a wheel with slots cut at increasing distances, which spaces the blows so the clock strikes one at one o'clock and twelve at twelve o'clock. The countwheel is the oldest striking control and predates the rack and snail.

Mechanism: When the strike is released, a lever rides on the countwheel's rim and drops into a slot after the correct number of blows, locking the train. The slots are cut deeper for later hours, so the lever falls further and later as the hours advance.

Maintenance: If a countwheel clock strikes the wrong hour, do not move the hand alone; let it strike through the sequence or turn the countwheel by hand to the correct slot. A bent lever or a dirty slot is the usual cause of miscounts.

Build and restoration: Countwheel repair means cleaning the slots and checking the lever's drop at each hour. Tools: tweezers, oil, screwdrivers, magnification, and a strike chart.

title: The Striking Bell
body:
Specifications: A lantern clock strikes on a single bell mounted on top of the movement, under the dome or fretwork. The bell is typically 8 to 12 centimetres across, cast in bell metal, and its tone is part of the clock's character.

Mechanism: A hammer lifted by the strike train falls on the bell once per blow, and the bell rings freely because it is mounted clear of the case. The hammer's fall distance sets the loudness, and the bell's size and metal set its pitch.

Maintenance: Keep the bell free of dust and check that the hammer falls squarely on the bell's sound bow. A hammer that strikes the bell's edge gives a dull sound and can crack the bell over time.

Build and restoration: Bell repair is limited to hammer adjustment, since a cracked bell cannot be safely re-tuned. Tools: hammer-setting gauge, screwdrivers, oil, and a pitch reference.

title: Alarm Lantern Clocks
body:
Specifications: Some lantern clocks carry an alarm: a second bell and a setting disc that releases the strike train at a chosen hour, ringing until the weight runs down or the owner stops it. Alarms were fitted for waking and for marking work hours.

Mechanism: The alarm disc is set by hand to the wanted hour, and a lever from the motion work releases the alarm train when the hour hand reaches the disc's notch. The alarm rings on its own bell, distinct in tone from the hour bell.

Maintenance: Set the alarm disc in the evening and test it once by hand before relying on it. If the alarm fails to ring, the disc notch or the release lever is usually dirty or bent.

Build and restoration: Alarm repair means cleaning the disc and lever and testing the release at every hour. Tools: screwdrivers, tweezers, oil, and an alarm test chart.

title: The Brass Case: Pillars, Frets, and Finials
body:
Specifications: A lantern clock's case is its movement frame made visible: four turned brass pillars at the corners, joined by top and bottom plates, with pierced brass frets in the sides and a finial on top. The frets let the bell sound out and let the owner see the movement.

Mechanism: The pillars are screwed into the plates and carry the whole movement, so a bent pillar throws the trains out of alignment. The frets are pierced by hand with scrolls, flowers, or dolphins, and each maker's fret pattern is distinctive.

Maintenance: Dust frets with a soft brush, never a cloth that snags in the piercing, and keep the pillars tight. A loose pillar is tightened by its screw, not by bending it back.

Build and restoration: Fret repair uses matching brass and soft solder, with the pattern followed exactly. Tools: soft brush, screwdrivers, soft solder, and magnification.

title: Lantern Clocks and the Chamber Clock
body:
Specifications: The chamber clock is a close cousin of the lantern clock, also weight-driven and brass-framed, but smaller and made to stand in a bedroom, often with a handle for carrying. Chamber clocks are sometimes called bedside lantern clocks, but they are a distinct smaller form.

Mechanism: Chamber clocks use the same verge and foliot or verge and pendulum movement as lantern clocks, in a frame about 20 to 25 centimetres tall, with a handle on top and a bell for striking. Their smaller size made them cheaper and more portable.

Maintenance: Care is the same as for a lantern clock: level placement, regular winding, and gentle brass cleaning. The handle must be checked before carrying, since a loose handle drops the clock.

Build and restoration: Chamber clock repair follows lantern clock practice, with smaller parts. Tools: screwdrivers, soft brush, oil, tweezers, and magnification.

title: Pendulum Conversions of Lantern Clocks
body:
Specifications: Many surviving lantern clocks were converted from foliot to pendulum regulation in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, when the pendulum's accuracy made foliot clocks seem crude. A conversion adds a pendulum, usually a long one hanging below the clock, and replaces the foliot with a crutch.

Mechanism: The conversion keeps the verge escapement but changes its regulation: the pendulum's swing now sets the beat instead of the foliot's inertia, and the clock's accuracy improves from a quarter hour a day to a few minutes a week. The original foliot parts were often discarded, which is why unconverted clocks are rare.

Maintenance: A converted clock must hang so the long pendulum swings freely below it, clear of the bracket and the wall. Wind it on schedule and keep the pendulum suspension spring clean and undamaged.

Build and restoration: Converting a foliot clock today is a specialist job that should be recorded, since it changes the clock's historical state. Tools: pendulum rod, suspension spring, crutch, screwdrivers, and a beat amplifier.

title: Anchor Conversions of Lantern Clocks
body:
Specifications: A further conversion replaced the verge escapement with an anchor escapement and a pendulum, giving lantern clocks the accuracy of contemporary longcase clocks. Anchor conversions are less common than verge-pendulum conversions and are usually later.

Mechanism: The anchor rocks with the pendulum and its pallets alternately catch the escape wheel, giving a steadier beat than the verge. The conversion requires a new escape wheel and anchor, fitted to the existing plates, and the dial may gain a minute hand at the same time.

Maintenance: Anchor-converted clocks are regulated like any pendulum clock, by the rating nut, and they keep time to a minute or two a week. Keep the anchor pallets lightly oiled and the pendulum suspension undamaged.

Build and restoration: Anchor conversion parts must match the existing plates, and the work should be documented. Tools: anchor, escape wheel, screwdrivers, oil, beat amplifier, and a timing chart.

title: Dating a Lantern Clock
body:
Specifications: A lantern clock is dated by its dial engraving, its fret pattern, its pillar shape, and its movement: early clocks have foliots and single hands, later ones have pendulums and minute hands, and the maker's name and town narrow the date further.

Mechanism: The chapter ring's lettering style, the centre engraving, and the fret design all changed over the seventeenth century, and reference books list makers and their working dates. A clock with a maker's name can often be dated to within a decade.

Maintenance: Record the clock's features, including any conversion, before cleaning, since cleaning can remove dating evidence such as wax in the engraving. Never remove a maker's name or re-engrave a dial to make it look sharper.

Build and restoration: Dating uses magnification, reference books, and comparison with dated examples. Tools: magnification, reference books, camera, notebook, and a soft brush.

title: Maintaining a Lantern Clock
body:
Specifications: A lantern clock needs winding daily or every few days according to its drop, regular dusting of the brass and frets, and a full service every five to eight years. The weights, lines, and bell need checking at each winding.

Mechanism: The going train runs from the weight barrel through the wheels to the verge or anchor escapement, and wear shows first at the barrel pivots. A clock that stops, strikes wrongly, or gains wildly usually has dirt, wear, or a damaged line rather than a broken wheel.

Maintenance: Between services, wind regularly, keep the clock level, and listen for changes in the beat or strike. Do not oil a dirty movement from the outside, since fresh oil on dirt spreads abrasive paste.

Build and restoration: A service bench needs a movement holder, cleaning jars, bushing tools, and an oil set. Tools: screwdrivers, tweezers, pegwood, bushing machine, pivot polisher, and clock oil.

title: Restoring a Lantern Clock
body:
Specifications: Restoring a lantern clock means returning it to working order while keeping as much original material as possible: cleaning the movement, re-bushing worn pivots, repairing frets and pillars, and leaving the dial engraving untouched. Later conversions are preserved and documented, not reversed without a reason.

Mechanism: Each train is stripped, cleaned, and reassembled in order, and worn pivot holes are bushed with brass rather than drilled oversize. The strike train is tested through all twelve hours before the clock is returned to its case.

Maintenance: Document every part replaced and every conversion found, with photographs before and after. A restoration that hides its own work misleads the next owner and damages the clock's historical value.

Build and restoration: Restoration tools include a bushing machine, a pivot polisher, and a strike test chart. Tools: bushing machine, pivot polisher, screwdrivers, tweezers, oil, and a camera.

title: Building a Replica Lantern Movement
body:
Specifications: A replica lantern movement is built from brass plates, turned pillars, a crown wheel and verge, and weight barrels, following the layout of a seventeenth-century original without copying any single maker's engraving or fret pattern. The replica is for study and demonstration, and it is marked as a replica.

Mechanism: The plates are cut and drilled from a layout, the pillars are turned and screwed in, and the trains are assembled and tested by hand before the dial is fitted. The verge and foliot are made first, since their geometry sets the rest of the movement.

Maintenance: Test the replica by hand at every stage, and mark it clearly as a replica on the back plate. A replica that is not marked will mislead future owners and collectors.

Build and restoration: Workshop tools include a lathe, a milling machine, files, and a depthing tool. Tools: lathe, files, depthing tool, screwdrivers, oil, and an engraving stamp for the replica mark.
